hops.title: Say it: blue jays are acorn gardeners
hops.text: Tell your child, "Blue jays are acorn gardeners. They hide acorns to eat later, and the ones they leave behind can grow into oak trees!" Use it when your child asks how a heavy nut travels. A jay can carry five acorns at once, fly them more than a mile, and bury up to 5,000 in one fall.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, "Species Spotlight - Oaks" (updated January 15, 2025)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A blue jay perched on an autumn oak branch with an acorn in its beak and fallen acorns below.
image.caption: Blue jays bury acorns to eat later, and some they leave behind sprout into new oaks.

hops.title: Point at it: the hooks and loops on a shoe strap
hops.text: Before you head out, pull open the hook-and-loop strap on your child's sneaker together. Let them find the stiff, scratchy hooks on one side and the soft loops on the other. In 1941, burdock burrs stuck to an engineer's pants and his dog's fur, and their tiny hooks gave him this idea. NASA has used it on spacecraft walls.

sources.citation: National Inventors Hall of Fame, "How Did a Walk in the Woods Lead to the Invention of VELCRO Fasteners?"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sneaker with its hook-and-loop strap opened beside a fuzzy wool sock holding a round burdock burr.
image.caption: Burdock burrs grab with tiny hooks, the same kind of grip that holds a sneaker strap shut.

hops.afterHeading: Questions to ask while you do it
hops.title: Compare it: a coconut has its own swim vest
hops.text: After the float test, tell your child that a whole coconut comes with its own puffy swim vest. Its thick husk and hollow center help it bob along on ocean waves. Scientists report that coconuts could still sprout after floating in seawater for up to 110 days. That is more than three months at sea!

sources.citation: Harries, H. C. & Clement, C. R. (2014), "Long-distance dispersal of the coconut palm by migration within the coral atoll ecosystem," Annals of Botany 113(4): 565-570, via NIH PMC

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A whole fibrous coconut floating on blue-green ocean waves near a sandy beach.
image.caption: A coconut's thick husk works like a swim vest, helping it float on long ocean trips.

audio.title: Three fun ways to talk about traveling seeds
audio.transcript:
If you are about to head out on the sock walk, here are three easy lines you can tuck in your pocket for the trip.

First, while your child is putting on shoes, pull open a hook-and-loop sneaker strap or jacket tab together. Let them touch the stiff, scratchy hooks on one side and the fuzzy loops on the other. Back in nineteen forty-one, an engineer came home from a walk with burdock burrs clinging to his pants and his dog's fur. Looking closely at those tiny hooks gave him the idea for hook-and-loop tape, a kind of grip NASA has used to hold gear on spacecraft walls. Suddenly that fuzzy sock on your child's shoe is not just a silly costume. It is a seed-catching experiment.

Second, if your child wonders how heavy seeds like acorns move without wings, try saying, "Blue jays are acorn gardeners!" A single blue jay can carry five acorns at once, fly them more than a mile away, and bury up to five thousand in one autumn. Jays hide acorns to eat later, and the ones they never dig back up can sprout into new oak trees.

Finally, after the float test, tell your child that a whole coconut wears a built-in swim vest. Its thick husk and hollow center help it bob along on ocean waves. Scientists report coconuts that could still sprout after floating in seawater for up to one hundred ten days.

Pick whichever line fits your moment, and enjoy watching what hitches a ride home.
